reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Gastric diverticulum is a rare outpouching of the stomach wall, with the great majority being congenital true diverticula located on the posterior wall of the gastric fundus just below the oesophagogastric junction.
The characteristic juxta-cardial posterior fundal location and its cystic appearance can mimic an adrenal mass, pancreatic pseudocyst or other retroperitoneal lesion on cross-sectional imaging.
Acquired diverticula are less common, usually located in the antrum or prepyloric region, and tend to be pulsion or traction type related to adjacent inflammation, ulcer or prior surgery.
Most gastric diverticula are asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic they cause vague epigastric or postprandial pain, dyspepsia, nausea or a sensation of fullness.
Complications, though uncommon, include bleeding from mucosal ulceration within the sac, perforation and, rarely, malignancy arising in the diverticulum.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with retroflexion in the fundus, or barium study, confirms the diagnosis and helps distinguish it from an extrinsic mass.
Because it can be mistaken for an adrenal or pancreatic lesion, awareness prevents unnecessary intervention; oral contrast filling the sac on imaging is a helpful clue.
Symptomatic or complicated diverticula are treated with surgical resection, increasingly by laparoscopic diverticulectomy, while asymptomatic lesions are managed conservatively.
reference.pathophysiology: Gastric diverticula are either congenital or acquired. Congenital (true) diverticula contain all layers of the gastric wall and typically arise on the posterior fundic wall near the cardia, at a point of relative muscular weakness where the longitudinal and circular muscle layers are deficient and where extraperitoneal support is limited. Acquired diverticula are usually false (pulsion) diverticula, in which mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscular wall in response to raised intraluminal pressure, or traction diverticula caused by external scarring from adjacent inflammatory processes such as peptic ulcer, pancreatitis or prior surgery; these are more often antral or prepyloric. Retention of food and acid within the sac may lead to mucosal inflammation, ulceration and, rarely, bleeding or perforation. The characteristic posterior juxta-cardial position of congenital diverticula explains why they are readily mistaken for retroperitoneal or adrenal lesions on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: adrenal mass or adenoma on cross-sectional imaging
gastrointestinal stromal tumour or submucosal gastric mass
additionalInvestigations: upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with fundal retroflexion
barium meal to demonstrate contrast filling the sac
computed tomography with oral contrast to confirm communication with the stomach
endoscopic ultrasound to assess wall layers and exclude a submucosal mass
cross-sectional imaging to distinguish from adrenal or pancreatic lesions
biopsy of the diverticular mucosa if malignancy is suspected
redFlags: gastrointestinal bleeding or melaena from the sac
severe or acute abdominal pain suggesting perforation
weight loss or a mass raising concern for malignancy
rapidly enlarging or irregular lesion on imaging
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent for the majority of asymptomatic diverticula managed conservatively, and surgical resection of symptomatic lesions is generally curative. Malignant transformation is rare but carries the prognosis of the underlying tumour.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing a posterior fundal diverticulum as an adrenal or pancreatic mass and pursuing unnecessary intervention.
Failing to retroflex in the fundus at endoscopy and missing the diverticular opening.
Attributing non-specific dyspepsia to the diverticulum without excluding commoner causes.
Overlooking bleeding or ulceration within the sac as a source of occult blood loss.
Not considering malignancy in a symptomatic or atypical diverticulum.
